findings.location: exceptions[3] (the five-day paragraph); forms_records[4]; timing_deadlines[5]; ma_vs_federal[1]-[2]
findings.problem: The section states the whole Massachusetts partial-fill regime from M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) alone and never reaches 105 CMR 721.055, the Department of Public Health regulation that implements it. 721.055(A) states the five-day initial-partial-fill limit by a different and broader operative test than the section teaches, and states it in calendar days: 'If the Prescription was issued by a prescriber from a location other than the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, as indicated by the address of the prescriber on the Prescription, the Prescription must be presented for initial partial fill not later than five calendar days after the Prescription issue date.' The section instead teaches that the five-day limit 'reaches only a prescription filled under subsection (d) or (d1/2)'.
findings.rationale: The regulation's trigger is the prescriber's address as it appears on the prescription, which is the fact a pharmacist actually checks; the statute's trigger is the subsection under which the prescription is being filled. The two converge on ordinary facts (both reach an out-of-state prescriber) and the section's gloss on s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) does convey 'out-of-state practitioner', so the practical answer is normally the same and no practice question is put at risk. But the word 'only' is narrower than the operative Massachusetts rule, the 'five calendar days' measure is not stated, and 105 CMR 721.055(B) and (C) - the regulatory statement of the same-pharmacy restriction, the 30-day remainder and the patient-record notation on both the initial partial fill and the remainder - are attributed to the statute alone. A section titled for Massachusetts Schedule II partial fills should cite the regulation that governs them.

findings.location: learning_objectives[3]; forms_records[1]-[2] and [6]; role_duties (all four entries)
findings.problem: Learning objective 4 declares that the section states 'what the partial-fill record must contain in each pathway', and the pharmacist's 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(5) notations and dispensing record are set out in full. The practitioner-side content of the same request-based record is missing. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3) requires that, where a practitioner wants a Schedule II prescription partially filled, 'the practitioner must specify the quantity to be dispensed in each partial filling on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the record for an electronic prescription', and 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(4) then bars the patient, a minor's parent or guardian, or a named caregiver from requesting more than the practitioner specified. Neither appears. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1)(iv), that 'the total quantity dispensed in all partial fillings does not exceed the total quantity prescribed', is also never stated, although learning objective 1 is to distinguish a prohibited refill from a lawful remainder and that cap is the boundary.
findings.rationale: The gap is systematically on the prescriber's side. role_duties assigns four duties and every one of them is to the Pharmacist, so the section names no prescriber duty at all, and the one prescriber duty it does carry - the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) Schedule II opioid notation - is stated in the passive voice ('A Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid must itself carry the notation') inside a records block whose other entries are pharmacist record-keeping. common_traps[5] does make clear that the notation sits on the prescription rather than in the pharmacy record, so no actor is misassigned, but a candidate is left without the practitioner's per-fill quantity specification that 1306.13(b)(3) makes part of the request-based record, and without the total-quantity cap. decision_logic[0] does convey the cap operationally ('The original Schedule II quantity was fully dispensed - do not process an additional dispensing as a refill'), which keeps the severity low and leaves every listed practice question answerable.

results.summary: I re-derived every legal proposition in this section from primary sources and found no false statement. 21 CFR 1306.13(a), (b)(1)-(b)(5) and (c) are reproduced accurately, including the three distinct clocks, the emergency-oral 72-hour carve-out inside the request-based pathway at 1306.13(b)(2), the 'terminally ill'/'LTCF patient' notation whose absence deems the prescription filled in violation of the Act, and the per-fill LTCF record of date, quantity dispensed, remaining quantity authorized and dispensing pharmacist. The section's central Massachusetts teaching is correct and I verified it independently: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) makes a written or electronic Schedule II prescription invalid 30 days after issuance with no LTCF, hospice or terminal-illness qualifier anywhere in c. 94C or in 105 CMR 700.000, so the federal 60-day figure in 21 CFR 1306.13(c) cannot be worked past day 30 on a Massachusetts prescription. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) reads exactly as the section says, including that the five-day initial limit attaches to a prescription 'filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2)', and s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) are correctly identified as the nonnarcotic out-of-state and the narcotic Maine-or-contiguous-state pathways. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) is quoted correctly. All eight listed practice questions (MA-Q-0011, 0012, 0021, 0094, 0160, 0161, 0401, 0432) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it; MA-Q-0160's federal 60-day answer is expressly reconciled with the Massachusetts ceiling rather than left in conflict. Two additions are needed before publication, both low severity: the section should cite 105 CMR 721.055, whose five-calendar-day trigger keys on the prescriber's non-Massachusetts address shown on the prescription rather than on the statutory filling subsection, and it should carry the practitioner-side content of the request-based record - 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3)'s per-fill quantity specification, (b)(4)'s cap on a patient's request, and (b)(1)(iv)'s total-quantity cap - and name the prescriber as the actor for the s. 22(c) notation.

findings.location: timing_deadlines[1] ('Massachusetts follow-up after any oral controlled-substance prescription, practitioner holding no s. 23(h) exception' / 'An electronic prescription within 2 days' / 'This is the shortest period reaching an emergency oral Schedule II prescription in Massachusetts'); quick_review[3]; ma_vs_federal[1]; common_traps[0]
findings.problem: The section installs a 2-day electronic follow-up under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) as the operative Massachusetts period for an emergency oral Schedule II prescription, calls it 'the shortest period reaching an emergency oral Schedule II prescription in Massachusetts', and warns the candidate that 'reaching for a seven-day figure on a Massachusetts emergency oral question' is the trap. On Massachusetts emergency-oral facts the 2-day branch of s. 20(c) does not apply at all, and the correct follow-up period is seven business days, capped by the shorter federal seven days. The section therefore teaches the candidate to reject the right answer and choose a wrong one.
findings.rationale: Section 20(c) sets the 2-day electronic follow-up as its default and diverts to a written follow-up 'within a period of not more than 7 days or such shorter period that is required by federal law' where 'the practitioner has received an exception from using an electronic prescription from the commissioner pursuant to subsection (h) of section 23'. Section 23(h) directs that 'the commissioner, through regulation, shall establish exceptions ... The exceptions shall be limited to: ... (iv) prescriptions that are issued or dispensed in emergency situations as defined by the commissioner'. The commissioner did exactly that: 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) lists 'Prescriptions issued or dispensed in Emergency Situations in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060' as one of the enumerated ePrescribing exceptions, and 105 CMR 721.020(A) makes every prescription generated in the Commonwealth an Electronic Prescription 'unless it is a Prescription issued in accordance with an exception listed in 105 CMR 721.070'. A lawful Massachusetts emergency oral Schedule II prescription is therefore always issued under a s. 23(h) exception, so it is the proviso rather than the 2-day default that reaches it. 105 CMR 721.060(A) then closes the loop expressly: an Emergency Situation waives only the electronic prescribing system requirement, and the resulting written and oral prescriptions 'must comply with all other Prescription requirements, including requirements outlined in 105 CMR 721.070(B)' - the seven-business-day (or shorter federal) follow-up. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the same seven-business-day count directly for this exact prescription. The Department's own guidance leaves no room: 'an oral prescription for a controlled substance in Federal schedule II-V issued in an emergency situation must be followed within seven business days by a written or electronic prescription for the emergency quantity', and 'if a prescriber fails to issue a follow-up written or electronic prescription within seven business days, the pharmacist is required to notify the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) of such failure'. The same guidance says that because the original prescription was issued under an ePrescribing exception, 'the expectation is that most follow-up prescriptions will be written rather than electronic' - the opposite of the electronic-within-2-days duty the section makes central. The section's own reasoning that the federal seven days under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) caps the seven business days is sound; the error is that it demotes that correct answer to an 'outer bound rather than extra time' and promotes a period that never reaches the facts.

authorities.exact_section: Circular DCP 19-12-108, 'Written or Electronic Follow-Up Prescription' and 'Emergency Prescribing of Schedule II Controlled Substances'

findings.location: decision_logic[3] ('You are asked how long the practitioner has to deliver the follow-up'); ma_vs_federal[2]
findings.problem: The section's decision rule is that 'the answer turns on whether the practitioner holds an electronic-prescribing exception', but the section never supplies the single fact that decides it on emergency-oral facts: that an Emergency Situation is itself one of the enumerated ePrescribing exceptions under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h)(iv). The candidate is handed a two-branch test and no way to select the branch on the facts the section exists to teach.
findings.rationale: The section holds the premise and draws the opposite conclusion. ma_vs_federal[2] states that 'Massachusetts frames the emergency as a waiver of the requirement to use an electronic prescribing system, so written and oral prescriptions become available while every other prescription requirement continues to apply' - which is 105 CMR 721.060(A), the provision that routes the emergency prescription straight into 105 CMR 721.070(B)'s seven-business-day follow-up. Yet timing_deadlines and common_traps resolve the branch the other way. A candidate who applies the section's stated rule faithfully will notice the emergency is a waiver and answer seven; the section tells that candidate they have fallen into a trap. The decision logic is internally unresolvable as written and the section resolves it wrongly.

findings.problem: The section names the 'defined emergency' and 'emergency situation' threshold four times without ever conveying its content, and the two sovereigns define it differently, so the section both leaves its first learning objective unmet and omits a real Massachusetts-versus-federal distinction.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 290.10, which 21 CFR 1306.11(d) incorporates, requires that the prescribing practitioner determine that immediate administration is necessary, that no appropriate alternative treatment is available including administration of a drug that is not a Schedule II controlled substance, and that it is not reasonably possible to provide a WRITTEN prescription before dispensing. 105 CMR 721.001 requires that immediate administration be necessary and either that it is not reasonably possible to generate or transmit an ELECTRONIC Prescription before dispensing or that the electronic prescription requirement would result in a delay adversely impacting the patient's medical condition. The Massachusetts test has no 'no appropriate alternative treatment' element and is keyed to the electronic rather than the written prescription; both tests reach a Massachusetts emergency oral Schedule II prescription. Learning objective 1 declares that the section lets a candidate 'state the conditions that let a pharmacist dispense a Schedule II substance on an oral authorization'; with the threshold left as a bare label the candidate cannot state them, and cannot see that the two definitions differ.

findings.problem: forms_records[1] attributes both 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and 'the date of the oral order' on the face of the follow-up to the Massachusetts rule as well as the federal one. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) requires only that the follow-up have 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' written on its face; the date of the oral order is a federal requirement under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4). The distinct Massachusetts face notation - that the prescription is 'issued to document an oral prescription' under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) and 105 CMR 721.070(B) - is stated only in a separate entry and not joined to the emergency follow-up.
findings.rationale: Nothing is lost operationally, because both sovereigns' requirements apply and a compliant follow-up therefore carries both notations. The mis-attribution matters only for a question that asks which sovereign imposes which notation, and would be corrected by a single clause. Recorded at low severity so the record is complete; it does not on its own change the disposition.

Circular DCP 19-12-108, Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual - 'Written or Electronic Follow-Up Prescription'; 'Emergency Situations'; 'Emergency Prescribing of Schedule II Controlled Substances'

results.summary: The federal half of this section is accurate. I checked 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(1)-(d)(5) line by line and the section reproduces the emergency-period quantity limit, the identity check for an unknown prescriber, the immediate reduction to writing with everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires except the signature, the 7-day follow-up, the 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' face notation and the date of the oral order, the postmark rule, the attach-or-annotate duty on receipt, the central fill prohibition in (d)(5), and - unusually well - the consequence the regulation attaches to the pharmacist's own omission, that failure to notify the nearest DEA office 'shall void the authority conferred by this paragraph to dispense without a written prescription'. Its paraphrase of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) is textually faithful and 105 CMR 721.070(C), 721.020(F) and 721.040(A) are quoted correctly. The Massachusetts half fails. The section makes a 2-day electronic follow-up the operative Massachusetts period for an emergency oral Schedule II prescription, labels it 'the shortest period reaching an emergency oral Schedule II prescription in Massachusetts', and tells the candidate that reaching for a seven-day figure is the trap. That is backwards. Because 105 CMR 721.070(A)(4) makes an Emergency Situation one of the enumerated ePrescribing exceptions established by the commissioner under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(h)(iv), and 105 CMR 721.020(A) permits an oral prescription in Massachusetts only under such an exception, every lawful Massachusetts emergency oral Schedule II prescription falls in the proviso of s. 20(c), not its 2-day default. 105 CMR 721.060(A) routes the emergency prescription expressly into 105 CMR 721.070(B), and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) states the count directly: seven business days, capped by the shorter federal seven days. The Department of Public Health says the same in Circular DCP 19-12-108 and adds that, the original prescription having issued under an ePrescribing exception, 'the expectation is that most follow-up prescriptions will be written rather than electronic'. The defect is architectural rather than local - it runs through quick_review, ma_vs_federal, decision_logic, timing_deadlines and common_traps - so the section needs a rewrite of its Massachusetts timing analysis, not an edit. Two further gaps: neither the federal 21 CFR 290.10 nor the Massachusetts 105 CMR 721.001 definition of an emergency situation is conveyed, although learning objective 1 promises the conditions and the two definitions differ; and the follow-up face notations are partly mis-attributed between sovereigns. MA-Q-0104 remains answerable from the section and is not contradicted by it - the DEA-notification duty and the expiry of the federal 7-day period are both correctly stated - so practice mapping passes.
